strategy_title: Avoid Autotune Configs That Cause Register Spill
strategy_description: Adding a @triton.autotune decorator with large XBLOCK configs (512–2048) caused the compiler to select a config that increased registers per thread from 17 to 48, triggering Block Limit Registers to drop from 21 to 5 blocks/SM and capping theoretical occupancy at 62.5%. Despite eligible warps per scheduler improving (1.17→5.26) and warp cycles per instruction decreasing (14.46→9.69), the 7.5x increase in executed instructions (18M→137M) caused duration to balloon from 41 µs to 193 µs — a 4.7x regression. The autotune decorator itself, combined with the introduction of a non-trivial xmask guard (replacing tl.full True mask), appears to have caused the compiler to generate a much more instruction-heavy kernel body for the winning config.
fast_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (baseline) - hardcoded XBLOCK=128, 17 regs/thread
@triton.jit
def kernel(in_out_ptr0, in_ptr0, ..., xnumel, XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xmask = tl.full([XBLOCK], True, tl.int1)  # trivial mask, no bounds check
    tmp0 = tl.load(in_out_ptr0 + x2, None)
    ...
    tl.store(in_out_ptr0 + x2, tmp17, None)
# Result: 17 regs/thread, Block Limit Registers=21, 18M instructions, 41 µs
applicable_when: Never apply this exact pattern (autotune with large XBLOCK + replacing None mask with xindex<xnumel guard) when the baseline kernel uses trivial masks (None/tl.full True) because xnumel is exactly divisible by XBLOCK.
do_not_apply_when: Do not add @triton.autotune with large XBLOCK configs when: (1) the baseline kernel uses None/trivial masks that the compiler can optimize away — replacing them with xindex<xnumel forces bounds-check codegen that dramatically increases register pressure and instruction count; (2) register count is already low (≤20 regs/thread) and the kernel body is simple — autotune may select a config that causes register spill, collapsing Block Limit Registers and negating any latency-hiding benefit; (3) xnumel is exactly divisible by all candidate XBLOCK values, making the mask change unnecessary.
framework_notes: Triton-specific: replacing `tl.load(ptr, None)` with `tl.load(ptr, xmask)` where xmask=xindex<xnumel forces the compiler to emit predicated/masked instructions even when the mask is always True at runtime. This can significantly increase register pressure and instruction count. Keep masks as None when xnumel is divisible by XBLOCK. The autotune decorator itself does not cause register spill — the mask change in the kernel body is the likely culprit.

strategy_title: Autotune larger XBLOCK causes register spill and instruction bloat
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512–2048) caused the compiler to allocate more registers per thread (17→32) and more than doubled the executed instruction count (18M→40M), increasing kernel duration by 44% despite improving occupancy (55%→87%). The root cause is that larger tile sizes force the compiler to keep more live values in registers simultaneously, increasing register pressure and instruction count beyond the latency-hiding benefit. When the original kernel is already compute-bound at small tile sizes with low register usage, increasing XBLOCK via autotune can backfire by inflating instruction count more than it reduces stall cycles.
fast_pseudocode:
# Before (faster) - fixed XBLOCK=128, no autotune
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xmask = tl.full([XBLOCK], True, tl.int1)  # no boundary check needed
    tmp0 = tl.load(ptr + x2, None)
    # ... same arithmetic ...
    tl.store(ptr + x2, result, None)
# grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
# registers_per_thread=17, executed_instructions=18M, duration=41.38us
applicable_when: Never apply this pattern when the kernel has very low register usage (≤20 registers/thread) and the instruction count is already minimal; increasing XBLOCK will inflate both.
do_not_apply_when: Do not increase XBLOCK via autotune when: (1) the kernel body has many live temporaries that scale with tile size, (2) the original register count is already low (≤20), suggesting the compiler is tightly optimized for the small tile, (3) xnumel is already evenly divisible by the current XBLOCK (no boundary waste). The instruction count increase from larger tiles can dominate over latency-hiding gains.
framework_notes: In Triton, adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs can unexpectedly double register usage because the compiler must handle boundary masks (xindex < xnumel) and keep more values live across the larger tile. The grid lambda must also be updated to use meta['XBLOCK'] when autotune is used. The implementation flaw here is that the grid was NOT updated to use meta['XBLOCK'] (still hardcoded to cdiv(xnumel, 128)), meaning autotune selected a larger XBLOCK but the grid remained sized for XBLOCK=128, causing each CTA to process only 128 elements despite XBLOCK being larger — this is an implementation bug that wasted compute.
